summary: For ages 6-8, sorting matures into organising AND recording categorical data: starting from a genuine statistical question, children sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list, and order the categories by quantity. The new skill beyond the 5-6 level is that the count becomes a written record that can be read back to answer the question — the table is a tool, not a decoration. Teaching should begin from a real question (e.g. 'which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table with totals that reconcile against the whole set, and always return to the question.
misconceptions: Records counts that don't line up with their categories (rows misaligned in the table)
Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table treated as decoration)
Miscounts categories or the totals don't reconcile with the full set
Forces every item into the given categories (or invents overlaps) when some items fit none

activities.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question
steps: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
activities.insight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.

activities.title: Interactive reconcile-and-order check (optional self-check mechanism)
steps: Drag each response card to a category pile and watch a tally build
Type each count into a table's cells
Notice when the row counts are flagged for not reconciling with the number of cards, and fix the lost or double-counted response
Press an 'order' control and watch the rows rank themselves most-to-fewest, lifting the winning category to the top
Answer a final question — which category answers our question?
activities.insight: A live record stays trustworthy only when its parts reconcile with the whole; ordering the rows turns the record into a visible answer.

activities.title: Read a completed table to say what it means (annotation scaffold)
steps: Look at a completed, labelled frequency table of category names and counts
Point to each row and say what it means ('this row says 5 children chose banana')
Say which row has the biggest count and what question that answers
activities.insight: Reading a table back — pairing each label with its count and identifying the largest — is a necessary step toward using data to answer a question.

checkQuestion: Our question is: which of these three fruits does our class like best? Here are everyone's choice cards. Organise them so we can answer the question, and show me the counts in a table. (Set the task and WATCH how they organise and record.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: sorts all cards into the three fruit categories, counts each, writes each fruit name beside its correct count in a table (totals reconciling with the number of cards), orders the categories, and states which fruit answers the question.
